scope: Scene-local provider word times and measured sound durations for the five GEMM regression scenes. Each scene starts at zero. Full-film offsets are outside this measurement.

changed.previousSay: In our scalar FP32 shared-memory model, thirty-two banks cycle through four-byte words. Bank number is word address modulo thirty-two. Several lanes reading the same word can broadcast; different words in one bank require separate service groups.

Let lane l read word thirty-two times l plus k. Thirty-two distinct words land in bank k: a thirty-two-way conflict in this model. Add one word of row padding and bank becomes l plus k modulo thirty-two, spreading the lanes. Padding changes row alignment and consumes capacity; a conflict degree is not itself a measured kernel slowdown.

An XOR layout stores logical column at column XOR row, using the same word count. Producers and consumers must use the same permutation. In row one, logical columns zero, one, two and three become physical one, zero, three and two. A vector copy from the first mapped address does not preserve logical order by itself. Check the actual vector or matrix instruction’s layout, not just this scalar access.

Register blocking gives each thread several output accumulators. For a one-by-four tile, one A value and four B values supply four multiply-adds. That is eight FLOPs from twenty operand bytes, or zero point four FLOP per byte. A scalar output uses two floats for two FLOPs, giving zero point two five.

For an eight-by-eight register tile, eight A and eight B values supply sixty-four multiply-adds: one hundred twenty-eight FLOPs from sixty-four operand bytes, or two FLOPs per byte. These are nominal per-thread operand-demand ratios. Broadcasts and generated instructions determine physical shared-memory traffic.

More live answers consume registers. That can reduce resident blocks or cause spills, while reuse can still help. Inspect the compiled resource report, occupancy limits and measured bottleneck together. High occupancy alone is not the objective.

Immediately above one thousand twenty-four, neighboring FP16 values are one unit apart. A positive quarter-unit update rounds away under round-to-nearest, while FP32 retains it. Immediately below that boundary the spacing is one half, so a negative zero point three seven five rounds to one thousand twenty-three point five. This is absorption by rounding, not subnormal underflow.

Use two numerical references. First round inputs to the kernel’s input format, then accumulate those rounded inputs in a suitable higher precision. That isolates arithmetic fidelity. Separately accumulate the original inputs in higher precision to include input quantization loss.

With A equal to one point zero zero zero one, one and B equal to one, minus one, FP16 rounds both A entries to one. A correct rounded-input result is zero, while the original result is about one ten-thousandth. The kernel can have zero error against its arithmetic reference and one hundred percent relative error against the original result. Wider accumulation cannot recover the lost input difference. Use absolute and relative tolerances, especially near cancellation, and check downstream quality separately.

A roofline ceiling is the smaller of peak compute and bandwidth times arithmetic intensity. Use FLOPs and bytes at the same declared boundary. A source-level load count is not automatically HBM traffic, because caches and reuse intervene.

For invented hardware with two hundred teraFLOPs per second and one terabyte per second, the ideal HBM knee is two hundred FLOPs per byte. A kernel at ten HBM FLOPs per byte has an ideal bandwidth ceiling of ten teraFLOPs per second. This upper bound does not establish its actual limiting stall or achievable throughput.

Validate reference outputs, edge shapes, strides and precision before timing. Warm up, synchronize the device timer, record shape and math mode, and distinguish kernel-only timing from conversion, padding and copies. CPU index checks verify the address model; a real GPU run and profiler evidence are needed for hardware performance claims.

You can now explain a tiled matrix multiply as a conservation of contributions. Each output receives every required inner-coordinate product. The execution plan changes where inputs wait and how many outputs can use them before they are replaced.

Try a new inner width of five with two-coordinate input panels. How many panels are needed, and how many coordinates belong to the last? Pause. Two full panels and one single-coordinate remainder still supply every required product exactly once. Retain the same output accumulators until all three contributions arrive.

The same principle appears throughout efficient machine learning: arrange the work so that a value earns its transfer by serving several dependent operations. Once the dataflow is visible, the equation on the page becomes an execution plan you can reason about and improve. Low-precision GPU programming next audits the operands entering those products, including encoding, scale scope and rounding that wider accumulation cannot undo.

beats.say: Inside shared memory, consecutive four-byte words cycle through thirty-two banks. If every lane reads word three, bank three can broadcast it once. Now give the lanes different words. Three, thirty-five and sixty-seven all leave remainder three when divided by thirty-two. They need separate service from the same bank.

A column with a stride of thirty-two words stacks all thirty-two requests in bank three. Add one word of row padding. Lane one now reads word thirty-six in bank four. Each lane lands in its own bank. Padding costs space and changes row alignment. The stack counts service groups for this scalar access. A profiler can tell you what it costs in time.

Another layout keeps the same space and changes the address with a bitwise exclusive or, called XOR. Watch row one swap its neighbors. To read the logical vector in order, visit physical columns one, zero, three and two. A four-word read starting at physical column one would grab the wrong sequence. The writer and reader need the same mapping.

Give four of those answers to one thread. For one reduction step, one A value and four B values supply four multiply-adds. That's eight FLOPs from twenty operand bytes, or zero point four FLOP per byte. With just one output, the thread reads two floats for two FLOPs, or zero point two five.

Now give that thread eight rows and eight columns. Eight A and eight B values feed every crossing. Sixty-four multiply-adds give one hundred twenty-eight FLOPs from sixty-four bytes. That's two FLOPs per byte. We're counting the operands a thread asks for. Broadcasts can change the traffic that shared memory actually serves.

The thread must keep sixty-four sums alive, along with its operands and indices. If registers run short, fewer blocks may fit, or the compiler may spill values to memory. Check register use in the compiled kernel and look for spills in the profile before increasing the tile again.
Both sums start at one thousand twenty-four. Add a quarter to each. The yellow tick marks the exact sum. Which stored value will move?
Store both results. FP32 moves to the yellow tick. FP16 stays at one thousand twenty-four. Its next value above here is a whole unit away, so the starting value is closer.

Reset both sums. This time subtract three eighths. Store the two results again. FP32 keeps the exact sum. FP16 lands at one thousand twenty-three and a half. The spacing below the boundary is only half a unit. The earlier quarter disappeared when the sum was rounded.

What if the difference disappears before the multiply? Take one point zero zero zero one and one as the two entries of A. B subtracts the second from the first. Keep one copy of the original FP32 inputs. Convert the other copy to FP16. Both entries of A are now one. Accumulate both references in double precision.

Suppose the kernel returns zero. Compare it to the lower reference first. The rounded-input result is zero. Against the original inputs it misses the entire difference. The original result is about one ten-thousandth. That's one hundred percent relative error for this small output. Use an absolute tolerance near zero as well as a relative tolerance. Check application quality separately.
Remember the thread that kept four answers? It got eight FLOPs out of twenty operand bytes. Can we put its zero point four on a graph of FLOPs per byte of high-bandwidth device memory?

We still need the bytes that crossed device memory. Count those bytes for the same launches as the FLOPs. Now we have the horizontal coordinate. Multiply by peak bandwidth to get a ceiling on work per second. The arithmetic units impose a second ceiling. The lower of the two forms the roof of this plot.

Suppose the device can do two hundred teraFLOPs per second and move one terabyte per second. The two ceilings meet at two hundred FLOPs per byte. Now place a kernel at ten HBM FLOPs per byte. It has an ideal bandwidth ceiling of ten teraFLOPs per second. A measured run can fall well below that line.

Start with correct outputs on edge shapes and nonsymmetric inputs. Match the layout, operand precision and math mode. Warm up, then time repeated launches with CUDA events in one stream and wait for the ending event. Record which copies and conversions the timer includes. A CPU index check can explain a missing product. Hardware counters and timings tell you whether a change helped on the GPU.

Here's a different edge. Keep two output columns, but give A just one row and five inner positions. Panels are two positions wide. The lower-right thread still has no output. How many panels cover those five positions? Which B entries must it load for the top-right answer?

Group the five positions. Two full panels and one single-coordinate remainder. The lower-right thread takes the second B row in each panel and column one. It loads four at position one and minus two at position three. In the final panel its B address falls past the end, so it fills that shared slot with zero.
Follow those loads into the neighbor's sum. Minus one plus eight gives seven in the first panel. The next adds zero and minus two, leaving five. There's still one real pair to add.

The upper-right thread loads the last four. One times four brings the top-right answer to nine. The bottom-right thread skips its store. Its neighbor gets the right answer because that thread stayed for the loads. In low-precision GPU programming we'll follow those same operands and ask what survives when their format changes.
